items.title: What Actually Makes an Act "Non-Dharma," and Doctrine Eight Closes

items.zh: 我今當說非法之相。若業，損他而不治現過，是名非法。又若業，諸修道者共知此業感不愛果，又若業，一切智者決定說為不善。又若業，自所不欲。又若業，染心所起。又若業，待邪呪術方備功驗，又若業，自性無記。諸如是等皆是非法。
items.en: I shall now state the mark of what is non-Dharma. Any deed that harms another without correcting an actual present fault is non-Dharma. Further, any deed that practitioners of the path uniformly recognise as bringing an undesirable result; any deed that every possessor of complete wisdom firmly declares unwholesome; any deed one does not oneself desire; any deed arising from a defiled mind; any deed that depends on a false mantra merely to seem effective; and any deed that is, by its own nature, karmically neutral — all such deeds are non-Dharma.

items.title: The Ninth Doctrine: Is the World Bounded or Boundless? A Cosmic Cycle Misread

items.zh: 邊無邊論者，謂如有一，若沙門、若婆羅門，依止世間諸靜慮故，於彼世間住有邊想、無邊想、俱想、不俱想，廣說如經。由此起如是見，立如是論：世間有邊、世間無邊、世間亦有邊亦無邊、世間非有邊非無邊。
items.en: The doctrine of a bounded or boundless world: there are certain renunciants or brahmins who, relying on worldly meditative concentration, come to hold, regarding that world, a notion of it having limits, of it being boundless, of it being both, or of it being neither — stated in full as in the sūtra. On this basis they arrive at this view and establish this doctrine: that the world has limits, that the world is boundless, that the world is both bounded and boundless, or that the world is neither bounded nor boundless.

items.zh: 當知此中，已說因緣及能計者。是中
若依斷邊際求世邊時，若憶念壞劫，於世間起有邊想。若憶念成劫，則於世間起無邊想。若依方域周廣求世邊時，若下過無間更無所得，上過第四靜慮亦無所得，傍一切處不得邊際；爾時則於上下起有邊想，於傍處所起無邊想。若為治此執，但依異文，義無差別，則於世間起非有邊非無邊想。
items.en: When seeking the world's limit through the boundary of its cessation: recalling a destruction-eon gives rise to the notion the world has limits. Recalling a formation-eon gives rise to the notion it is boundless. When instead seeking the world's limit through the extent of its regions: finding nothing below beyond the Avīci hell, nor anything above beyond the fourth dhyāna, yet finding no limit at all extending sideways, one arrives at a notion of limits above and below but boundlessness to the sides. And, merely to answer this last position with different wording rather than any different meaning, one arrives at the notion that the world is neither bounded nor boundless.

items.zh: 今應問彼：汝何所欲？從前壞劫以來，為更有世間生起？為無起耶？若言有者，世間有邊，不應道理。若言無者，非世間住，念世間邊，不應道理。如是彼來有故，彼來無故，皆不應理，是故此論非如理說。
items.en: One should press them: what do you actually intend — since the last destruction-eon, has the world arisen again, or not? If it has arisen again, then calling the world "bounded" makes no sense, since it plainly continues on. If it has not arisen again, then there is no world at all to speak of — so debating whether it is bounded or boundless makes no sense either. Thus, whether the world has arisen again or not, neither position holds up, and so this doctrine is not a soundly reasoned teaching.

items.title: The Tenth Doctrine: "Deathless" Evaders Who Never Give a Straight Answer

items.zh: 不死矯亂論者，謂四種不死矯亂外道，如經廣說應知。彼諸外道，若有人來，依最勝生道問善不善，依決定勝道問苦集滅道，便自稱言：不死亂者。隨於處所，依不死淨天不亂詰問，即於彼所問，以言矯亂，或託餘事方便避之，或但隨問者言辭而轉。
items.en: The doctrine of evasive equivocation about the deathless: this refers to four kinds of non-Buddhist teachers who equivocate about the deathless, as stated in full in the sūtra. Should anyone come to question these teachers about what is wholesome or unwholesome via the path to a favourable rebirth, or about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path via the path of decisive liberation, they simply declare: "I am one who is deathless and unerring." Yet wherever they are, when questioned without confusion by one of the truly pure, deathless heavens, they answer with deliberate equivocation, or divert to some unrelated topic to avoid the question, or simply echo back whatever words the questioner themselves used.

items.zh: 是中，第一、不死亂者，覺未開悟；第二、於所證法起增上慢；第三、覺已開悟而未決定；第四、羸劣愚鈍。
items.en: Among these: the first kind of "deathless equivocator" has simply never awakened to any real understanding at all; the second harbours an inflated conceit about what they have actually attained; the third has genuinely awakened to some understanding but remains undecided and uncertain; and the fourth is simply feeble-minded and dull.

items.title: Three Kinds of Fear Behind the Evasion

items.zh: 又復第一，怖畏妄語及怖畏他人知其無智，故不分明答言我無所知。第二，於自所證未得無畏，懼他詰問，怖畏妄語，怖畏邪見，故不分明說我有所證。第三，怖畏邪見，怖畏妄語，懼他詰問，故不分明說我不決定。如是三種，假託餘事以言矯亂。
items.en: Further: the first, fearing to speak falsely and fearing others will discover his ignorance, will not plainly say "I know nothing." The second, having no real confidence in what he has attained, dreads being questioned — fearing to speak falsely, and fearing to be exposed as holding a wrong view — and so will not plainly say "I have attained something." The third, fearing to be exposed as holding a wrong view, and fearing to speak falsely, dreads being questioned, and so will not plainly say "I remain undecided." All three, in this way, divert to unrelated topics and answer with deliberate equivocation.

items.title: The Fourth Equivocator, and Doctrine Ten Closes as a Fearful, Deceitful View

items.zh: 第四，唯懼他詰，於最勝生道及決定勝道皆不了達，於世文字亦不善知，而不分明說言我是愚鈍，都無所了。但反問彼，隨彼言辭而轉，以矯亂彼。此四論發起因緣，及能計者，并破彼執，皆如經說。由彼外道多怖畏故，依此見住。
items.en: The fourth simply dreads being questioned at all: understanding neither the path to a good rebirth nor the path of decisive liberation, and not even skilled in ordinary worldly language, he will not plainly admit "I am dull and understand nothing at all." Instead, he merely questions the questioner back, and simply echoes whatever words come back to him, thereby equivocating. It is because these non-Buddhist teachers harbour so much fear that they cling to this view at all.

items.zh: 若有人來有所詰問，即以諂曲而行矯亂。當知此見是惡見攝，是故此論非如理說。
items.en: Whenever anyone comes with a genuine question, they respond only with flattering, crooked, evasive words. This view should be understood as belonging among the wrong views, and so this doctrine is not a soundly reasoned teaching.

items.title: The Eleventh Doctrine: Everything Arises Without Any Cause At All

items.zh: 無因見論者，謂依止靜慮，及依止尋思。應知二種如經廣說。問：何因緣故，彼諸外道依止尋思，起如是見，立如是論：我及世間皆無因生？答：略而言之，見不相續以為先故，諸內外事無量差別種種生起。或復有時，見諸因緣空無果報。
items.en: The doctrine positing no cause: this arises both from reliance on meditative concentration and from reliance on ordinary reasoning, as stated in full in the sūtra. Stated briefly: this arises from first observing a lack of continuity, whereby countless different internal and external phenomena appear to arise, and, at times, from observing what seem to be causes and conditions producing no actual result at all.

items.zh: 謂見世間，無有因緣，或時欻爾大風卒起，於一時間寂然止息；或時忽爾瀑河彌漫，於一時間頓則空竭；或時欝爾果木敷榮，於一時間颯然衰顇。由如是故，起無因見，立無因論。
items.en: That is: they observe, apparently without any cause at all, a great wind suddenly rising and then, at some point, falling utterly still; a raging river suddenly swelling and then, at some point, running abruptly dry; or trees and fruit suddenly flourishing in lush abundance and then, at some point, withering all at once. It is on this basis that they arrive at the view of no cause, and establish the doctrine of no cause.

blocks.text: Today's reading covers three doctrines briefly. Before them, the treatise gives a short definition of what makes an act "non-Dharma", which is worth more than the doctrines themselves. Then come the view that the world is bounded or boundless, the "evasive equivocators", and the opening of the view that things arise without any cause.
Untranslated: 0310a26 ("here the causes and those who hold the view have been explained") and 0310c20–c23 (a summary of why no-cause fails).

The marks of non-Dharma begin with harming others "without correcting a present fault". Venerable Miào Jìng: "If my act removes my own greed, hatred, and delusion, that's 'correcting a present fault.'" They include acts one would not wish done to oneself. Master Cháng Bǎi, citing the *Pīxún jì*: a deed that brings inner sorrow and regret is non-Dharma. Together these give a working test: an act is wrong if it harms others without curing my own afflictions, if I would not want it done to me, or if it leaves me with regret.

The ninth doctrine arises from "worldly meditative concentration", which Venerable Miào Jìng defines: the four dhyānas as attained by non-Buddhists, without the wisdom that makes them transcendent. A meditator who recalls a destruction-eon concludes the world has limits; one who recalls a formation-eon concludes it is boundless. Searching in space, they find limits above and below but none sideways, because, Venerable Miào Jìng explains, worldly powers cannot see beyond a middle-sized world-system.

The refutation: since the last destruction, has the world arisen again? If so, "bounded" in time fails; if not, there is no world to wonder about. Once again, a real meditative experience supports a false conclusion because it is partial.

The tenth doctrine belongs to teachers who never give a straight answer. "Deathless" (不死), Master Cháng Bǎi explains from the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, means the gods, whom outsiders take to be undying; these teachers claim to serve them. When asked about the path, they equivocate.

There are four kinds of equivocator: one who has never understood; one conceited about what he thinks he has attained; one who has understood something but is undecided; and one who is simply dull. Their evasion springs from fear: of being shown up, of saying something false, of being questioned further. The treatise calls it "a fearful, deceitful view".

Master Cháng Bǎi explains why study of these errors matters: "One's conduct can't go beyond one's thinking; wrong thinking means wrong conduct. Studying the outsiders' wrong ideas helps us avoid making the same mistakes." The equivocator is a useful mirror for any teacher who would rather sound profound than admit not knowing.

The eleventh doctrine: everything arises without any cause. It comes from meditation and from reasoning. Both teachers, following Kuījī and the *Vibhāṣā*, explain the meditative source. Someone reborn from the heaven of no perception, where they spent five hundred great eons without perception, can recall their past only as far as the moment perception returned, and so thinks they arose from nothing. The reasoners observe winds suddenly rising and falling still, rivers flooding and drying up, and conclude there is no cause. Tomorrow's reading refutes them.

quiz.q: The marks of non-Dharma begin with harming others "without correcting a present fault," and include "what one would not wish." How do the teachers read these?
options: Venerable Miào Jìng: "correcting a present fault" is curing one's own present greed, hatred, delusion; Master Cháng Bǎi, citing the Pixunji: "what one doesn't wish" is a deed that brings inner sorrow
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "If my act removes my own greed, hatred, and delusion, that's 'correcting a present fault.'" Master Cháng Bǎi: "A deed that brings inner sorrow and distress is 'what one doesn't wish.'" The translation's "one would not wish done to oneself" reads it as a golden-rule test, unlike the *Pixunji* (logged in the correction list).

quiz.q: According to the treatise, on what basis do the bounded/boundless theorists form their view?
quiz.why: "Relying on worldly meditative concentration, come to hold, regarding that world, a notion of it having limits, of it being boundless, of it being both, or of it being neither." Master Cháng Bǎi: though they attain absorption, attachment, views, conceit, and doubt remain uncut.

quiz.q: Seeking the world's limit by its cessation, how do the notions of "bounded" and "boundless" arise?
options: recalling a destruction-eon gives "bounded"; recalling a formation-eon gives "boundless"
quiz.why: "Recalling a destruction-eon gives rise to the notion the world has limits. Recalling a formation-eon gives rise to the notion it is boundless." Venerable Miào Jìng: recalling destruction, they haven't seen the next formation, so think "bounded"; seeing formation but not the destruction after, they think "boundless."

quiz.q: How does the treatise refute the bounded/boundless doctrine?
options: since the last destruction-eon, has the world arisen again? If yes, "bounded" fails; if no, there's no world to ponder
quiz.why: "Since the last destruction-eon, has the world arisen again, or not? If it has arisen again, then calling the world 'bounded' makes no sense … If it has not, then there is no world at all to speak of." Master Cháng Bǎi: if it re-forms after destruction, how can it end there? and if there's no world, how can it be bounded or not?

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what are the four kinds of deathless equivocators?
options: (1) not awakened; (2) conceited about attainment; (3) awakened but undecided; (4) feeble and dull
quiz.why: "The first … has simply never awakened to any real understanding at all; the second harbours an inflated conceit about what they have actually attained; the third has genuinely awakened to some understanding but remains undecided; and the fourth is simply feeble-minded and dull." Master Cháng Bǎi on the second: temporarily free of desire, yet claiming nirvāṇa; Venerable Miào Jìng: taking worldly dhyāna for the noble path.

quiz.q: Having covered these doctrines, why does Master Cháng Bǎi say studying non-Buddhist errors is worthwhile?
options: action never outruns thought — wrong thinking means wrong action; studying their errors keeps us from making them
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "One's conduct can't go beyond one's thinking; wrong thinking means wrong conduct"; "studying the outsiders' wrong ideas helps us avoid making the same mistakes." The text concludes this view belongs among wrong views.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, from what does the no-cause view arise?
quiz.why: "The doctrine positing no cause: this arises both from reliance on meditative concentration and from reliance on ordinary reasoning." Venerable Miào Jìng: reasoners have a sharp sixth consciousness; he cites Tang Junyi, who "spun a whole theory out of one small matter" — no absorption, but a keen mind.
